stories.topic: A Prediction Comes True: The India-UK Trade Deal
stories.summary: At the end of the second globalisation episode, Ajay predicted that good things were in store for India's trade policy. He based this on reading newspapers and 'understanding the chessboard', not on inside information. At recording time (May 8), the first piece had arrived: a free trade agreement with the UK. The newspaper reports describe tariff cuts on 90% of products and a 10-year glide path (he would have preferred five). By the end of the ten years, 80% of products reach zero tariff. UK companies will also be able to bid in Indian government procurement. He cautions that he has only read news reports, that you should always read the legal documents, and that the devil is in the details.
stories.insight: A credible, pre-announced glide path forces firms to take a hard look at themselves: raise productivity or go out of business. Cheaper imported raw materials make other Indian firms more competitive. Opening procurement means taxpayers' money buys steel for a police station at the lowest price. And zero tariffs with one country weaken the case for tariffs with everyone else, so one deal can cascade.
stories.quote: Also, once you've got zero tariff with one country, what's the point of having tariffs with anybody else?

stories.topic: The Bank That Wanted Its ATM to Dispense a Five Star
stories.summary: Many years ago, a bank wanted to coax customers away from branch counters and towards ATMs. Its idea was to stock Cadbury Five Star bars inside the ATM, so that any withdrawal above Rs 5,000 would also spit out a chocolate. Sad story number one: the bank had to seek the regulator's approval. Sad story number two: approval was denied, because handing out candy along with cash was 'undignified'. Ajay notes it may not work this way today.
stories.insight: This is intrusive central planning in miniature. A product decision that should be the firm's own business judgment became a permission slip. When everything is banned by default, innovation depends on a regulator's taste.
stories.quote: Like this is the business judgment of the firm. It should be the birthright of the firm.

stories.topic: How a 2012 Paper Woke Up a 'Clueless Economist'
stories.summary: Ajay personally knows many of the people who laid the foundations of RBI and SEBI. He calls them wonderful people who meant well. But they lacked the knowledge, and they recklessly fused legislative, executive and judicial powers into single agencies. The first person to see the problem was Dr. Sahu, who had worked in the Ministry of Finance, SEBI and the Competition Commission, and became the first chairman of the bankruptcy regulator. In 2012 he wrote a paper and started giving talks pointing out that this violated separation of powers.
stories.insight: This was a comprehensive intellectual failure. Philosophers, legal experts, political scientists and economists all missed a danger understood since the 17th century. Good intentions without knowledge produce bad institutions, which is why Ajay says a country can only be as good as its thinkers.
stories.quote: And for me it was just like wow, how did I not know this? I was a clueless economist

stories.topic: Dr. Sahu Puts Checks on Himself at IBBI
stories.summary: The team that drafted the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code had imported FSLRC's 140 sections on how a regulator should work. Inside the government, those sections were deleted and replaced by 'the bad 15 sections from the SEBI Act'. When Dr. Sahu became the first chairman of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, the law imposed no checks on him. He knew that would go badly, so he created checks himself. He split IBBI internally into legislative, executive and judicial departments. Around 2016 or 2017, the IBBI board enacted a regulation governing how IBBI makes regulations, importing a subset of the FSLRC procedure. This mirrored the semi-legal agreements between the Finance Ministry and RBI that came before proper law.
stories.insight: When you can't fix the law, a reformer who holds power can still fix the practice by binding himself. That voluntary practice can later become a template for others.
stories.quote: So he did separation of powers inside the IBBI.

stories.topic: FSLRC: The Unenacted Law That Seeded Reforms
stories.summary: In 2011, finance minister Pranab Mukherjee kicked off the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission. It was begun by KP Krishnan in the Department of Economic Affairs and chaired by Justice Srikrishna. Ajay faced 'the only job interview of my entire life', conducted by Justice Srikrishna, and went on to co-lead the technical team with Ila Patnaik. The commission produced a clean modern law to replace sixty bad financial laws, including 140 sections of general regulatory theory. It processed about 800 public comments over a four-year project (2011–2015). The law-drafting team was trained by one of the world's top law drafters. Ten years later the law has not been enacted. But ideas incubated inside it, such as inflation targeting and a monetary policy committee, later became a separate law.
stories.insight: By one measure the project failed. Ajay argues that this measure is wrong: democracies don't progress through one cathedral project. Progress comes from building intellectual products and persuading, until ideas creep into practice one by one.
stories.quote: I was made to face the only job interview of my entire life.

stories.topic: Mango Season: RBI Agrees to Rules on Making Rules
stories.summary: IBBI's self-imposed rule-making procedure sat alone for years. Then SEBI issued its own regulation on how it makes regulations, importing the same bag of ideas. On the morning of recording, Ajay got an SMS that RBI had done the same. Three regulators now have board-approved regulations governing their own regulation-making. Ajay stresses this is not the end. A board binding its own staff is weaker than Parliament binding the agency. And it will take another decade to build the state capability needed, such as civil servants who understand market failure and cost-benefit analysis.
stories.insight: A journey that began in the 2000s has reached a milestone in 2025. Nobody in good faith can now claim that a regulator should have unchecked power to make regulations. It shows the hosts' theory of change in action.
stories.quote: At this point, I think the intellectual argument has been won.

stories.topic: David Stockman's Despair in Reagan's Washington
stories.summary: In Government's End, Jonathan Rauch recalls arriving in Washington in the mid-1980s and chatting with David Stockman, Reagan's man. Reagan's rhetoric promised to make government small and lean. Yet Stockman was depressed and bitter: they had come with such good intentions, and it was so hard to get anything done. Later, Bill Clinton and Newt Gingrich each tried in their own ways to do the same thing, and both failed.
stories.insight: Demosclerosis is structural, not partisan. Once interest groups and regulations pile up, they defeat even reformers at the very top, from either party.
stories.quote: He is a president's man, imagine it's hard for the president to get anything done.

stories.summary: When the Shah Rukh Khan film Raees came out, Amit wrote that it got basic economics wrong. In the film, a politician tours town campaigning for prohibition, and Shah Rukh's bootlegger character tries to stop him. But a bootlegger's business only exists because of prohibition.
stories.insight: This is Bruce Yandle's Bootleggers and Baptists in pop culture. The moral crusader and the profiteer are natural allies. When you see a campaign for a ban, ask who profits from it.
stories.quote: And I'm like, wait a minute. You know, it is in the bootlegger's interest to have prohibition because that is how his business flourishes.

recommendations.item: Regulation: A Primer
recommendations.creator: Susan Dudley and Jerry Brito
recommendations.context: At the end, Ajay asked Amit for a great book on regulation. Ajay then revealed it is Amit's loo reading.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a wonderful book. It is mostly about how regulation works in America, but the first and last chapters cover the general theory of regulation. It overlaps with what Ajay covered, though 'nowhere near as comprehensively'.

recommendations.item: Government's End: Why Washington Stopped Working
recommendations.creator: Jonathan Rauch
recommendations.context: Amit's history of regulatory thinking, on how interest groups took over American policymaking.
recommendations.reason: It 'blew my mind'. It coined 'demosclerosis': interest groups and regulations multiply until they become nearly impossible to reverse and crowd out other policymaking. It also tells the David Stockman anecdote.

recommendations.item: The Theory of Economic Regulation
recommendations.creator: George Stigler
recommendations.context: Amit tracing how thinking moved beyond public-interest theory and capture theory.
recommendations.reason: A famous 1971 essay with three axioms. The state has coercive power; private parties benefit from steering it; so every private party has a rational self-interest in trying to. It explains why lobbying is inevitable and why you must be super careful.

recommendations.item: Bootleggers and Baptists: The Education of a Regulatory Economist
recommendations.creator: Bruce Yandle
recommendations.context: Amit's discussion of how regulations actually get passed.
recommendations.reason: In Amit's words, 'a beautiful way of thinking about how regulation works'. The moralist and the profiteer lobby for the same ban, and sometimes the bootlegger openly funds the Baptist.

recommendations.item: Fortress and Frontier in American Health Care
recommendations.creator: Robert Graboyes
recommendations.context: Amit's example of regulation producing its own failure, via the FDA's slow drug approvals.
recommendations.reason: It gave Amit 'a new framework to think about the world'. Healthcare regulation is a high-walled fortress, while tech is an open frontier where anyone can try things. Amit notes its case is nuanced, not a call to scrap the FDA.

recommendations.item: Raees: An Empty Shell of a Gangster Film
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentioned his review while explaining Bootleggers and Baptists.
recommendations.reason: It shows how the film got prohibition economics backwards: the bootlegger should want prohibition, not fight it.

recommendations.item: The Baptist, the Bootlegger and the Dead Man Walking
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Show-notes link accompanying the Bootleggers and Baptists discussion.
recommendations.reason: Further reading from Amit on the same framework.

recommendations.item: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission (FSLRC) Report, Volume 1
recommendations.creator: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission
recommendations.context: Ajay explicitly recommends it to everybody while describing FSLRC. Amit says he will read it.
recommendations.reason: A crisp summary of 20 years of Indian research on regulation and regulatory theory. It is written as elegant, compact chapters, each ending in a box of drafting instructions for the law-drafting team.

recommendations.item: FSLRC Volume 2: The Indian Financial Code (draft law)
recommendations.creator: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission
recommendations.context: The draft law that came out of FSLRC.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it the cleanest, best-drafted modern law-drafting project in Indian history and a role model for how laws should be drafted. It also incubated ideas like inflation targeting.

recommendations.item: The LEAP Blog
recommendations.context: Ajay cites it, alongside working papers at NIPFP and IGIDR, as where research on India's regulators accumulated through the 2000s.
recommendations.reason: Part of the body of hundreds of blog articles and dozens of papers that built India's regulatory-theory literature behind FSLRC.

recommendations.item: Making Regulation in India Work Better
recommendations.creator: KP Krishnan
recommendations.context: Show-notes link. Ajay credits KP Krishnan with beginning FSLRC inside the Department of Economic Affairs.
recommendations.reason: A talk on fixing Indian regulation by the official who started the FSLRC project.

recommendations.item: Rethinking Regulation in India (talk and slides)
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Show-notes link to Ajay's talk and slideshow on Indian regulatory theory.
recommendations.reason: A fuller presentation of the regulatory-theory argument Ajay makes in this episode.

recommendations.item: A Deregulatory Moment
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Show-notes link to Ajay's Substack post.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's written take on the current opening for reforming India's regulatory state.

recommendations.item: The Administrative Procedures Act (1946)
recommendations.context: Ajay's model of a general law that disciplines all regulators at once.
recommendations.reason: 'A brilliant piece of law' ('Don't you envy these countries?'). It applies to all US federal agencies rather than one at a time. It came as a Republican pushback against the Democrats creating too many federal agencies. Court challenges under it built up a body of jurisprudence constraining regulators.

recommendations.item: Understanding the State (Episode 25 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Where Amit starts the conceptual build-up to this episode.
recommendations.reason: It covers the liberal purpose of the state: protecting our rights through the rule of law.

recommendations.item: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced as the basis for the market-failure discussion.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it Ajay's 'great masterclass' on the four kinds of market failure and when the state may intervene.

recommendations.item: Don't Punish Victimless Crimes (Episode 73 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced while explaining prohibition.
recommendations.reason: It covers why banning drinking doesn't solve the problem but creates an underground run by bootleggers.

recommendations.item: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited as a modern example of interest groups shaping the rules.
recommendations.reason: It recounts how the sugar lobby funded fraudulent studies from the 1950s to the 1980s suggesting sugar was fine and fat was the problem.

recommendations.item: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited when asking why a 'benevolent' government doesn't stop capture.
recommendations.reason: Governments are manned by people who respond to incentives, and nobody is omniscient. That is why government failure is ubiquitous.

recommendations.item: Rethinking Innovation Policy (Episode 59 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited when classifying which market failures call for regulation.
recommendations.reason: It explains why a positive-externality problem like building an R&D system is seldom a regulation problem.

recommendations.item: Separation of Powers (Episode 91 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced twice: on separation of powers, and on recent US developments around the SEC and Chevron Doctrine.
recommendations.reason: The foundation for seeing why regulators fusing legislative, executive and judicial powers is so dangerous.

recommendations.item: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Invoked as 'our theory of change episode' when explaining why FSLRC's unenacted law still mattered.
recommendations.reason: Progress is a story of intellectual persuasion, not one big cathedral project.

recommendations.item: Inflation Targeting Rocks! (Episode 68 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited as the biggest FSLRC idea that turned into reality.
recommendations.reason: Inflation targeting and a voting monetary policy committee were incubated inside the Indian Financial Code and later enacted separately.

recommendations.item: Going Bankrupt in India (Episode 80 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced in the story of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code's drafting.
recommendations.reason: Background on the IBC. Its first draft carried FSLRC's checks and balances on regulators before they were deleted.

recommendations.item: The Globalisation Episode and Is Globalisation Doomed? (Episodes 95 and 96 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The opening good news: Ajay's hopeful closing reading in the second episode is coming true with the India-UK FTA.
recommendations.reason: Shows the reasoning behind his prediction that India could seize this moment for globalisation.

recommendations.item: India's Massive Pensions Crisis (Episode 347 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's example when asking whether reforms like FSLRC are outliers.
recommendations.reason: A cautionary tale. A small intellectual community built the new pension scheme, and when it dispersed, institutional memory vanished and nobody was left to defend the reform.

core_ideas.concept: Rule of Law First; Competition Is the Best Regulation
core_ideas.explanation: The liberal paradox: we give the state a monopoly on violence, surrendering some rights so it can protect the rest through the rule of law. That means everyone knows the law, it applies equally, there is due process, the prosecutor isn't the judge, and the law is predictable. The rule of law also protects us from our protectors. Under it, sellers competing for a customer's money keep each other honest. Amit insists that rule of law and regulation are different things. The answer to 'evil capitalists' is a strong rule of law, after which, as Hayek argued, little regulation is needed.
core_ideas.quote: So in a marketplace which is functioning well, competition is the best regulation.

core_ideas.concept: Default Skepticism: Three Questions for Any Regulation
core_ideas.explanation: A market failure is necessary but not sufficient for intervention. Most of the time doing nothing is better, though some cases, like pollution beyond a point, do justify action. Amit's stance is to meet every proposed or existing regulation with extreme skepticism and ask three questions.
core_ideas.quote: The questions include who does this benefit, who does this hurt, and what are the unintended consequences down the road.

core_ideas.concept: Only Some Market Failures Call for Regulation
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's sorting: public goods call for the government to make or buy the good, not regulate. Positive externalities, like building an R&D system, call for voucher-type solutions. Negative externalities, asymmetric information and market power may justify coercing firms. Counting positive and negative externalities as halves gives his tally of 'one and a half' versus 'two and a half'.
core_ideas.quote: So for one and a half problems, it's not regulation. For two and a half it can be regulation.

core_ideas.concept: Regulation vs Regulators vs Regulatory Theory
core_ideas.explanation: Regulation is state coercion aimed at firms, rarely individuals. Regulators are specialised arms of the state that do regulation, but a government department can regulate too. Regulatory theory is the general technology that applies across airports, banks and drugs alike. Domain knowledge should be built on top of it.
core_ideas.quote: So regulators only do regulation, but not all regulation is done by regulators.

core_ideas.concept: Stigler's Axioms and Concentrated Benefits, Diffuse Costs
core_ideas.explanation: Stigler's three axioms: the state has coercive power, whoever steers it benefits, so every private party will rationally try. Public choice explains why this works. A tax or entry barrier that costs each citizen a rupee goes unnoticed, while the beneficiary collects a fortune and can share it with politicians. Each of us loses many such rupees without ever knowing.
core_ideas.quote: every regulation harms the people. But the cost is so small when you think of it in individual terms, and so invisible, the unseen, as it were, that we don't even notice

core_ideas.explanation: Jonathan Rauch's term for what happened in Washington. Interest groups and regulations multiply until they become almost impossible to reverse, and they crowd out the space for other policymaking. Presidents, Reagan's own man, Clinton and Gingrich all failed to roll it back.
core_ideas.quote: His point was what happens is that the interest groups just multiply, multiply, multiply, multiply.

core_ideas.explanation: Bruce Yandle's insight. A moral crusader (the Baptist) lobbies for prohibition, and the bootlegger, who profits from the ban, is his natural ally and sometimes his funder. Related modern examples Amit gives: tobacco companies supporting FDA pre-approval rules for new cigarettes because they create entry barriers, and the sugar lobby funding studies that blamed fat.
core_ideas.quote: So guess who are the two people who should technically be aligned here and often are? The Baptist and the bootlegger.

core_ideas.concept: Government Failure Is Ubiquitous, and Often Unseen
core_ideas.explanation: Public choice holds that bureaucrats want bigger budgets and departments, politicians want re-election, and nobody is omniscient. The FDA shows the seen and the unseen. The seen: approved drugs are safe. The unseen: rigid procedures delay approvals by seven or eight years and cost lives. In Graboyes' terms, regulated healthcare is a walled fortress, while tech is an open frontier.
core_ideas.quote: We talk about market failure, but market failure is rare. Government failure is ubiquitous.

core_ideas.explanation: From Hayek and Mises: each regulation creates downstream problems that invite more regulation. Rent controls cause housing shortages, which lead to housing subsidies, which lead to zoning laws, until everything 'starts to go to hell'.
core_ideas.quote: That regulation leads to downstream consequences which you have to solve for with more regulation and so on down the line.

core_ideas.concept: Separation of Powers: Only a Judge Should Be Able to Harm You
core_ideas.explanation: Since the 17th century, liberal democracy has worked by dispersing power. It is split between union, state and city, and between legislature (writes the law), executive (investigates and prosecutes) and judiciary (alone can punish). A citizen should be completely unafraid of civil servants and legislators.
core_ideas.quote: A civil servant should never have the power to punish you.

core_ideas.concept: The Regulator Bargain: Parliament and Police in One Agency, Surgically
core_ideas.explanation: Globally, regulators exist for two reasons. One is specialisation, unlike generalist ministries that rotate staff every five years. Ajay would prefer rotation across regulators over India's cradle-to-grave employment in one agency. The other is a deliberate breach of separation of powers: fusing law-writing with enforcement, as with the US SEC born in the 1930s. The UK's Financial Conduct Authority writes rules, polices and investigates, then takes cases to a tribunal. The bargain only works if Parliament delegates narrowly, one market failure at a time. The airport regulator should regulate monopoly returns, not be 'feudal lord of airports' deciding the colour of the mirrors in the loo.
core_ideas.quote: So it's like the police and the parliament have been fused into one agency and you can carry till prosecution.

core_ideas.concept: India's Three-Power Monster and the Silence of the Graveyard
core_ideas.explanation: Indian regulators like RBI and SEBI also took the judicial power to punish, on top of low rule of law. They have sweeping delegated law-making, licensing that can't be appealed, and opaque punishments. Regulated firms, whose survival depends on the regulator, stop speaking. They praise the regulator and lobby it to block rivals, killing competition, entry and innovation.
core_ideas.quote: You get a silence of the graveyard in the public domain.

core_ideas.explanation: Liberalisation is believed to have killed central planning. Instead, about 75% of the economy came under regulators, whose staff control products and internal processes more intrusively than the old, distant state ever did. A headline saying a regulator 'introduced' a product should make you see red. Ajay calls this one of the most important elements of how India lost the growth dynamic of 1991–2011.
core_ideas.quote: There is a deep misconception on the part of a lot of people that thanks to the 1991 reforms we got a great decline of central planning in India. This is largely not true because actually something like 75% of the economy came under the footprint of regulators.

core_ideas.concept: The Fix Lives in the Founding Law
core_ideas.explanation: There are three steps. First, narrow each delegation of law-making power into a precise section with an objective and balancing considerations. Second, wrap law-making and licensing in due process, including appeals against denials. Third, move the power to punish out to High Courts, as in the UK and Australia. XKDR Forum research suggests the Bombay and Delhi High Courts are improving. This is generic technology, so India could have a general law like America's Administrative Procedures Act.
core_ideas.quote: All this is actually generic. It is not about SEBI, it is not about FSSAI, it is not about RERA, it's actually a general technology.

core_ideas.concept: Earning Democratic Legitimacy for Unelected Rule-Makers
core_ideas.explanation: FSLRC's procedure for making a regulation runs as follows. A board with a majority of independent, non-civil-servant directors starts and ends the process. Staff write down the objective and demonstrate a market failure. They weigh six alternatives with cost-benefit analysis and pick the lowest-cost option that works. The draft goes out for 90 days of public comment, and the board revises it in light of the criticism.
core_ideas.quote: If we had any philosophers worth their salt in India, they should be standing up and saying, How dare you? You're an unelected official. How dare you have the power to write law?

core_ideas.concept: Theory of Change: Persuasion, Not Cathedrals
core_ideas.explanation: Reform rarely comes from one grand project being enacted. It comes from building intellectual products and persuading repeatedly until ideas creep into practice, as inflation targeting and regulators' rule-making procedures did. Foreign models can't be transplanted mechanically. You have to be rooted here and spend twenty years researching Indian conditions.
core_ideas.quote: The journey of progress is a story of intellectual persuasion.

core_ideas.concept: A Country Is Only as Good as Its Thinkers
core_ideas.explanation: India's 'doctor engineer' obsession starved law, philosophy, political science and public administration. What humanities exist often became a simplistic social-justice project rather than the study of how advanced economies became advanced. Law schools teach how to litigate a section, not how to design one. Designing law takes political philosophy, public administration, public economics and history: you need to know about the rise of Nazi Germany to think about surveillance. Lawyers should be the coders, with thinkers upstream.
core_ideas.quote: A country can only be as good as its thinkers.

core_ideas.concept: Research and Reform Communities Need Expertise and Staying Power
core_ideas.explanation: Reforms survive when a community of experts stays engaged for years. They write publicly and stay five, ten or twenty years ahead of officials, ready when problems become pressing. The pension reform shows what happens otherwise: the core group dispersed and nobody was left to defend it. Ajay rejects merely staffing today's officials, and tells young people that without mastery they have no business in public policy.
core_ideas.quote: If you will work to the agenda of today's joint secretary and today's secretary, then that's not progress. Then you're just being an HR staffing agency.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's opening: 'we have two pieces of good news for you, which are that I'm Amit and he's Ajay. No no no. We have two actual pieces of good news for you.'
Amit's blockbuster pitch for the India-UK FTA, 'Return to Zero': 'India invented zero, and now these tariffs are gonna go back to zero now. Now the foreigners are bringing zero back to India.'

Amit needles Ajay that decades of economists couldn't liberalise trade: 'Who got it done? Donald Trump got it done.' Ajay: 'Amitbhai, you and I should nominate Donald Trump for the Bharat Ratna.' Amit, hastily: 'He is joking... people are gonna like clip this and put this on Twitter and say he's a Trump bhakt.'
After Ajay's careful definitions, Amit says: 'I love the way you say regulation and regulator. I could listen to you all day.' Ajay apologises: 'forgive me, this is a lifetime of angst.'
A joke from Amit's friend about Washington DC: throw a stone in one direction and you'll hit a legal firm, throw it in another and you'll hit a lobbying firm.
Ajay on what surgical delegation should prevent: a regulator acting as 'feudal lord of airports', deciding 'what shall be the color of the mirrors in the loo'.
Amit's humblebrag while recommending Graboyes: he won the Bastiat Prize in 2014, 'the year before I won it for the second time.'
Amit to Ajay: 'You were a clueless economist in your words. I'm not calling you names.'
Amit on incremental reform: 'One baby step at a time, the infant crawls away from the precipice, but it can still hear the labored breathing of the monster.'
Amit, after hearing about the 25-year journey, on the show's own prospects: 'twenty-three years later Everything is Everything will have its first viral video. That is my hope.'
Behind-the-scenes clip on recommendations perpetually deferred to 'next episode': 'Every episode he does this. The sevens are multiplying. Compound interest.'
Amit on his book pick: 'this episode is actually the recommendation. So please watch this episode, but if you are watching this, you already have. So please watch it again.'

Ajay reveals Regulation: A Primer 'is sitting in his loo. It is his loo time reading.' Amit: 'you must have sneaked into my loo... at my home in Andheri... Please do not reveal any of the other books you saw there.'
Amit reaches for the classic maxim after Ajay's account of regulators' fused powers: 'power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely.'

Recent US developments recalled from the Separation of Powers episode: the right to a jury trial being used to knock out trials run inside the SEC, and developments around Chevron Doctrine. Courts are now 'all over the working of these regulatory agencies'.
Amit asks whether an economist really needs 17th-century political philosophy and even the Magna Carta, and answers 'frankly, yes': depth isn't enough without breadth.
